Chapter.Content: 02 — Surfaces, Topology and Parameterization
Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter

A surface has both local shape and global connectivity, and one representation rarely serves every operation equally well. This chapter builds the geometric and topological vocabulary used later for meshes, queries and simulation.
By the end: Choose between parametric, implicit and mesh representations based on the operation required.
Recall question: How do parameterization and topology answer different questions about a surface?
Surfaces, patches, topology, and parameterization
Surfaces combine local parameter domains with global topology, so geometry and connectivity must be reasoned about together.
Curves, surfaces, and local coordinates

A circle can be represented parametrically as or implicitly as . A parameterization generates points and supports traversal. An implicit equation supports inside-outside tests and level-set queries. For a surface parameterized by , tangent vectors are and ; their cross product gives a normal. For an implicit surface , the gradient gives a normal when nonzero. Different representations expose different operations naturally. CMU-09

A manifold is a space that locally resembles ordinary Euclidean space. A curve locally resembles a line; a surface locally resembles a plane. A coordinate chart describes a patch. The tangent space collects directions that remain on a surface to first order. A sphere cannot be mapped globally to one flat chart without seams or distortion, though small patches are locally planar. Singularities occur when a chosen parameterization collapses directions or an implicit gradient vanishes. CMU-09 · CMU-10
Orientability, boundaries, and local neighborhoods

Orientability means one can choose a consistent normal direction over the entire surface. For an orientable mesh, adjacent faces traverse their shared edge in opposite directions. A sphere and a torus are orientable; a Möbius strip is not. A boundary vertex has an open fan of incident faces; an interior vertex has a closed fan. At an interior manifold vertex, the incident faces form one cycle. At a boundary manifold vertex, they form one chain. Multiple disconnected cycles around one vertex signal a nonmanifold configuration.

Euler characteristic can detect topological changes. A closed sphere mesh with , , and has . A torus has characteristic 0. Splitting an edge in a way that preserves topology adds one vertex, two edges, and one face in a simple triangular setting, leaving unchanged. A careless collapse may merge distinct regions and change topology or create a nonmanifold vertex. This makes topological checks useful before and after mesh edits.
Parameterization distortions

Flattening a curved surface into a plane cannot preserve every geometric property globally. A conformal map preserves local angles but may change area. An area-preserving map retains area but can distort angles. Length-preserving maps are generally impossible for curved regions without special conditions. Texture artists often choose seams to divide a surface into charts and minimize distortion. Geometry-processing algorithms may choose a parameterization to reduce stretch or to make triangles closer to equilateral in the plane. The quality objective should follow the downstream use: texture appearance, finite-element conditioning, or atlas packing each values different properties.
Surfaces: parameter domains, patches, and meshes
A parametric surface maps a two-dimensional domain into three-dimensional space, . A tensor-product Bézier patch applies a one-dimensional basis independently in both parameters:

where is a grid of 3D controls and are cubic Bernstein basis functions. Fixing gives a curve in ; fixing gives a curve in . This makes the patch intuitive, but the rectangular parameter domain becomes awkward for complex topology, and stitching many independent patches while preserving derivative continuity can be difficult. The lecture walks through a bicubic patch, relating its rows and columns to families of Bézier curves, then discusses its patch-boundary continuity problem MITG-03 (00:47:00–01:01:00). The OCW 2012 lecture 02 is useful supplemental evidence for tensor-product patches and the Utah teapot example (pp. 24–34); its attribution/year must remain explicit.
The two parameter directions also give the local frame of the surface. Differentiate the tensor-product formula term by term:

points along the surface as changes while stays fixed; points along the other parameter direction. Their cross product is perpendicular to both, so the unit surface normal is . The direction depends on parameter orientation: swapping and flips the cross product. If is near zero, the parameterization is singular or locally collapsed; normalization then amplifies numerical noise, so a renderer must handle degenerate patches carefully.

For a numerical sanity check, consider the plane . Then , , and . The dot products with both tangent directions are zero: and . This cross-product construction is the same whether the surface is represented by a patch, a mesh’s local triangle, or a limit surface, though the derivative computation differs.

Joining two patches repeats the curve continuity problem along an entire boundary. If meets , position continuity requires equality for every boundary parameter . Matching to gives parametric first-derivative continuity across the seam; requiring only aligned tangent planes gives geometric smoothness. In a control grid, the boundary rows determine the seam, and the adjacent rows determine cross-boundary tangent direction and scale. A patch can therefore be smooth internally yet show a crack or shading seam when connected to a neighbor with mismatched boundary data.

Subdivision surfaces start from a coarse polygon mesh and repeatedly refine it. A typical step splits faces and edges, then relocates old and new vertices using local weighted averages. Repetition makes a smoother limit surface. Instead of requiring an artist to lay out a clean rectangular patch network, subdivision begins with a mesh whose connectivity can represent complex topology. The 2021 lecture compares Loop subdivision on triangular meshes and Catmull–Clark subdivision on polygonal meshes, emphasizing that the resulting smooth surface is understood as the limit of repeated local rules MITG-03 (01:02:00–01:15:00). The key design question is not merely “how many polygons?” but “what limit surface does this connectivity and stencil imply?” Irregular vertices need special care because their local neighborhoods do not resemble a regular grid.

This is a different kind of representation from a single analytic patch. A coarse control cage is both compact and topological: edges say which regions meet, while the subdivision rule defines how the cage smooths. A character’s elbow, for example, is awkward to cover with one rectangular patch network but natural as a polygonal mesh whose connectivity follows the limb. Refinement can be delayed until rendering, so the artist edits a manageable cage while the renderer evaluates a smooth limit. The costs are that the final surface may not interpolate the cage vertices and that extraordinary neighborhoods require special handling. The same refinement philosophy appears in adaptive curve drawing: preserve a high-level shape representation and create renderable detail only where the image needs it.

Implicit surfaces use a different representation: a scalar function and a level set such as . This can describe shapes without explicitly storing a mesh, but surface sampling and intersection are less direct. A parametric mesh offers explicit points and connectivity; an implicit model offers a compact inside/outside or field-based rule. The 2021 lecture briefly places implicit surfaces alongside patch and subdivision representations MITG-03 (01:13:00–01:17:00). The trade is between ease of expressing shape and ease of the later operation: rendering needs intersections or samples, while modeling needs intuitive control.
Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing
Reconstruction checkpoint — topology before surgery

The surrounding chapter explains half-edges, differential operators, remeshing and simplification; the new executable layer makes the first topology invariants inspectable. tools/labs/mesh_topology_lab.cpp builds directed and undirected edge records from triangles, pairs opposite half-edge twins, counts boundary and non-manifold edges, detects orientation conflicts, and checks Euler characteristic on both a two-triangle disk and a closed tetrahedron. A third construction deliberately creates an edge shared by three faces and must be rejected as non-manifold.

That is intentionally earlier than a QEM collapse loop. A simplifier must first prove that it knows what connectivity it is about to mutate. Half-edge topology invariants develops the representation contract, while QEM edge collapse and validity derives plane quadrics and explains why a low geometric error score cannot override link/manifold/orientation validity.

Rigid animation now has a separate representation witness as well. tools/labs/dual_quaternion_skinning_lab.cpp constructs dual quaternions from rotation plus translation, verifies rigid distance preservation, blends pure translations, and tests the antipodal sign case where physically equivalent dual quaternions would otherwise cancel. It does not yet claim arbitrary multi-joint GPU skinning or scale/shear; Dual quaternion skinning keeps that boundary explicit.
Meshes turn continuous shape into explicit data structures whose neighborhoods support edits, queries, and simulation.
Mesh topology and data structures

A triangle mesh stores vertices, edges, and faces. Geometry gives vertex positions; topology gives connectivity. A surface vertex is manifold when its incident faces form one disk-like fan, or one half-disk fan at a boundary. A bow-tie vertex where two fans meet only at one vertex violates the manifold condition even if all individual triangles are valid. Algorithms that assume one coherent local sheet can fail on such a mesh. CMU-10

An indexed-face array stores a list of vertex indices per triangle. It is compact for drawing but neighboring-face queries need extra work. A halfedge data structure stores each directed edge with a twin halfedge, the next halfedge around a face, and pointers to incident vertices and faces. It makes local traversal explicit. Boundary handling must be consistent, either with boundary halfedges or an exterior face. Orientation requires adjacent faces to traverse their shared edge in opposite directions. CMU-10

For a closed, connected, orientable surface, Euler characteristic is . For genus , : a sphere-like surface has characteristic 2 and a torus has 0. In a closed triangular mesh every edge belongs to two faces, so counting face-edge incidences gives . These identities help check connectivity, but do not by themselves prove manifoldness. CMU-10
Geometry processing and mesh edits
Smoothing reduces local variation. The umbrella Laplacian at vertex is the neighbor average minus the current point:

Moving vertices in this direction removes high-frequency noise but also shrinks convex shapes because neighbor averages fall inside the surface. Cotangent weights improve the connection to the continuous Laplace-Beltrami operator. For an edge opposite angles and , a common weight is . Negative weights can occur around obtuse triangles, and poor mesh quality affects the approximation. Denoising therefore requires more than averaging; constraints or feature-aware weights may be needed to preserve a silhouette. CMU-11

An edge flip replaces the diagonal shared by two triangles with the other diagonal of their quadrilateral. It preserves the same planar patch when the four vertices are coplanar and the quadrilateral is convex; for a non-convex quadrilateral, the alternate diagonal does not triangulate the same patch. The flip also must satisfy the mesh’s manifold and orientation constraints. An edge split inserts a new vertex and subdivides incident faces, increasing sampling. An edge collapse merges endpoints and removes faces, simplifying the mesh but possibly changing shape or violating manifoldness. Each operation has topological preconditions and geometric quality checks. Subdivision repeatedly refines faces and repositions vertices according to a scheme. Loop subdivision targets triangular meshes; Catmull-Clark handles polygonal faces. Repeated refinement approaches a smooth limit surface, unless boundary or crease rules preserve sharp features. CMU-11

Parameterization maps a surface patch into a plane. It supports texture coordinates and planar computation, but necessarily trades distortion in angle, area, or scale. Remeshing changes the sampling layout to improve triangle shape or local resolution. The mesh is not merely an approximation to a shape: its connectivity, attributes, and refinement rule influence the operations possible and the limit surface obtained. CMU-11
Local editing and quality measures

Triangle quality can be measured by minimum angle, aspect ratio, or area relative to edge lengths. Long thin triangles lead to poor interpolation and unstable numerical operators. Edge flips can improve local minimum angles in planar triangulations. Edge splits add resolution where error or curvature is high; collapses remove redundant detail. Remeshing combines these operations to achieve target edge lengths and better-shaped elements. A boundary or crease must be protected when edits would otherwise move it.

Smoothing with Laplacian displacement is a form of diffusion on a graph. For a graph Laplacian matrix , vertex coordinate matrix , and step size , explicit smoothing is . Large can oscillate or destabilize; repeated small steps attenuate high-frequency modes more gradually. Low-frequency shape modes decay too, which explains shrinkage. Solving an implicit step, such as , can improve stability while still smoothing. Feature constraints, volume-preserving updates, or curvature-aware weights can reduce unwanted shape loss. CMU-11
A local connectivity structure makes edits explicit

A polygon mesh combines geometry, such as vertex positions, with topology, such as which vertices bound each face. Keeping the two separate matters: the same connectivity can be embedded with different coordinates, and moving coordinates does not by itself change which faces are adjacent. A triangle soup stores three positions per triangle. It is simple input for a rasterizer, but shared vertices and their attributes are duplicated, and a neighborhood query must scan every face. An indexed mesh stores positions once and stores each triangle as three indices. This removes duplication but does not automatically make reverse adjacency fast. If a billion-face indexed mesh is queried for the few faces touching one vertex, a direct scan still checks a billion triples.

Incidence matrices make adjacency explicit. A vertex-edge matrix has a row for each edge and a column for each vertex; a one marks that the edge touches the vertex. An edge-face matrix marks which faces use which edges. These tables can answer neighborhood questions, but most entries are zero. Sparse formats store only nonzero entries. A coordinate map stores row, column, and value triples and is convenient to build or edit. A row list chains nonzero entries by row. Compressed column storage packs values and row indices into arrays and uses a cumulative offset array to locate each column’s range. The latter is efficient for matrix-vector products, but awkward for frequent insertions. Connectivity storage, like numerical storage, is a workload choice. CMU-10

A half-edge encodes directed adjacency with a small set of pointers. Every undirected edge becomes two oppositely directed half-edges. Each half-edge stores its twin (the opposite direction along the same edge), its next half-edge around the same face, the vertex it leaves, and references to its edge and face. Each face, edge, and vertex stores one representative half-edge. To list a face’s vertices, begin at its representative and repeatedly follow next until returning to the start. To circle a vertex, follow twin.next: cross the current edge to the neighboring face, then advance along that face to the next outgoing edge. For an interior manifold vertex this walks one complete fan. The method is efficient because it visits the local ring rather than scanning the whole mesh.

The pointer rules are topology invariants: following twin twice returns to the original half-edge; no half-edge is its own twin; and every half-edge belongs to a closed next cycle. Twin pairs encode undirected edges, next cycles encode faces, and twin.next cycles encode vertex neighborhoods. These invariants yield a manifold connectivity structure. They do not guarantee good coordinates. One may scramble the vertex positions so faces intersect, assign a quotient surface too few distinct positions so it collapses to a line or point, or have a geometrically skinny triangle whose connectivity remains valid. Debug connectivity and geometric quality as separate layers. CMU-10

The half-edge representation supports local edits by changing a bounded set of pointers. An edge flip replaces the shared diagonal of two triangles with the other diagonal of their quadrilateral; it changes connectivity but creates or deletes no elements. Performing the flip twice restores the original connectivity. An edge split inserts a vertex on an edge and replaces two incident triangles with four, so new faces, edges, half-edges, and a vertex must be allocated and connected. An edge collapse identifies the edge’s endpoints and removes the two incident triangles and other now-invalid elements. Each operation must restore every twin, next-cycle, face, edge, and vertex reference. Starting with the common case of an interior edge with exactly two incident triangles keeps the operation small and clear. A subdivision modeler uses these local operations to edit a coarse control cage; subdivision then generates a smoother surface. CMU-10
A mesh processing failure as a query problem

Suppose a geometry-processing operation downsamples a shape and then reconstructs it. The reconstructed surface may drift from the original. A signed-distance or closest-point query can measure this deviation. Sampling points on the original, finding nearest points on the reconstructed mesh, and accumulating distances creates an error metric. The result depends on sample density: sparse points may miss a narrow feature. Thus mesh quality, query acceleration, and numerical integration meet in one practical evaluation workflow. CMU-12
Why a mesh can be treated like a signal

A scalar image is sampled over a 2D grid. A mesh surface is sampled over a graph-like neighborhood. Vertex positions, normals, or colors are fields defined on that mesh. A discrete Laplacian compares each vertex’s value with its neighbors, analogous to a spatial high-pass operator on an image. Low-frequency variation corresponds to broad shape; high-frequency variation can correspond to noise or fine detail. Downsampling a mesh can remove detail and cause shape drift, just as downsampling an image can remove texture or create aliasing. A robust simplification method should preserve features that matter to downstream queries, not merely reduce vertex count.

For a mesh scalar field , a weighted discrete Laplacian at vertex has form . If neighboring values are equal, the Laplacian is zero. If one vertex differs sharply, the Laplacian magnitude is large. This operator can smooth color or geometry, estimate curvature, or build a diffusion process. The weights define what “neighbor influence” means and may account for edge length, angles, or local area. CMU-03 · CMU-11
Differential coordinates preserve local shape while solving for new global positions

Directly editing vertex positions makes global coordinates the primitive. Botsch and coauthors show another useful view: represent local shape through differential coordinates, modify those local quantities, then reconstruct positions by solving a sparse system.
For a piecewise-linear scalar function on a triangle mesh, its gradient is constant inside each triangle. Apply that independently to the three coordinate functions of the embedding,
and each face has a Jacobian built from the gradients of . A desired local rotation/scale/shear can be represented by a matrix , giving a target gradient
The modified gradients generally no longer integrate exactly to one globally continuous surface. Reconstruction therefore asks for vertex positions whose gradients match the targets in least squares:
The Euler–Lagrange equation has Poisson form,
which becomes a sparse linear system after discretization. Handle and fixed-region positional constraints remove the null modes and make the solution correspond to the user’s intended edit.

This gives a deeper interpretation of “Poisson mesh editing.” The linear solve is not smoothing by itself. The right-hand side encodes a desired local differential field; the solve finds the globally coherent surface closest to it. If the target field is inconsistent, the least-squares solution distributes the mismatch over the surface according to the operator and constraints.
Laplacian editing uses per-vertex differential coordinates
instead of per-face gradients. Transform them to , then seek positions whose Laplacians match those targets. In the continuous formulation Botsch et al. minimize
leading to a bi-Laplacian equation

The distinction matters. A first-order gradient formulation and a second-order Laplacian/shell formulation have different smoothness behavior at the boundary of the deformed region, different conditioning, and different sensitivity to constraints. “Both solve a sparse matrix” does not make them the same deformation model.

Rotations need special treatment. If one simply keeps the original Laplacian vector while rotating a handle by ninety degrees, local details resist rotation because the differential vector is expressed in the old frame. The source therefore propagates local transformations and applies them to gradients/Laplacians before reconstruction. Polar decomposition is useful here because rotation should be interpolated differently from scale/shear. A globally linear solver can thus participate in a geometrically nonlinear editing workflow by updating the local target frames.

This is also why the cotangent operator matters beyond smoothing. On irregular meshes, the uniform graph Laplacian depends strongly on valence and sampling density. Botsch et al. explicitly note improved deformation behavior from the cotangent discretization. The operator, mass weighting, constraints, and local-frame update together define the edit; none should be hidden behind the generic label “Laplacian deformation.”

Source basis: Botsch, Kobbelt, Pauly, Alliez, and Lévy, Polygon Mesh Processing, Chapter 9, especially §§9.4.1–9.4.3 on gradient-based deformation, Laplacian coordinates, Poisson/bi-Laplacian reconstruction, local transformations, and the relationship to shell-based deformation.
Parameterization distortion is a singular-value statement about the surface map
The current parameterization section says that angle, area, and scale cannot generally all be preserved. The differential-geometry formulation makes that trade measurable.

Let a local parameterization map a 2D parameter domain to a surface. Its Jacobian maps infinitesimal parameter-space directions into tangent vectors on the surface. Locally, a tiny circle in parameter space becomes an ellipse whose principal stretches are the two singular values
Those two numbers separate the common distortion goals.
A map is locally conformal when it preserves angles. Equivalently, the two principal stretches are equal:
A tiny circle stays a circle, though its radius may change. It is area preserving when
so the determinant of the local metric/Jacobian preserves area, though a circle may become an ellipse. It is locally isometric when both are true:
That preserves both angles and lengths locally. A general curved surface cannot be flattened isometrically; only special developable geometry permits it without cutting or distortion.

This turns UV quality into a local tensor measurement rather than a visual judgement. A texture can tolerate different errors depending on its content. Fine directional line art is sensitive to angular/shear distortion; a density map may care more about area; repeated texel detail may expose stretch. The correct objective follows the downstream signal.

Least-squares conformal maps formulate conformality as a least-squares condition on the gradients of the two UV coordinate functions. Harmonic/barycentric parameterizations solve related sparse systems under boundary constraints. The boundary treatment is not a cosmetic detail: fixing a poor boundary polygon can force interior distortion even when the interior solver is exact.

When a parameterization method reports one scalar “distortion,” ask which invariant it measures and in which map direction. Literature alternates between studying and its inverse . Singular values invert under map inversion, so formulas can appear contradictory when the convention is unstated.
Source basis: Polygon Mesh Processing, Chapter 5, especially conformal mapping and §5.5’s distortion analysis in terms of the first fundamental form and singular values.
Signed distance as a geometric signal

For a surface , signed distance field returns the shortest distance to the surface, positive outside and negative inside under one sign convention. The zero level set recovers the surface: . Near a smooth surface, the gradient of a true signed distance has unit length and points along the normal. This makes distance fields useful for collision margins, shape blending, and volumetric rendering. However, at points with multiple equally close surface points, distance may not be differentiable. In a mesh, approximate signed distance uses closest-point queries and inside-outside classification, combining geometric search with topology assumptions. CMU-09 · CMU-12
Subdivision masks and quadric error become executable rules
Subdivision masks and quadric error are computable rules, not labels
Loop subdivision: old vertices and new edge points

Subdivision repeatedly replaces a coarse mesh by a finer one and moves its vertices according to local weighted averages. The aim is a predictable smooth limit surface: the control mesh remains a compact description, while each refinement step supplies more triangles to represent the limit. Loop subdivision is designed for triangle meshes. One step splits every triangle into four: each old triangle retains one corner triangle near each old vertex, and a central triangle fills the middle. The new edge points must be placed with weights that account for the two triangles sharing an interior edge. CMU-11 (PDF pp. 25–26; video 00:34:30–00:37:00)

Here each lowercase letter denotes a 3D position vector. The weights sum to one, so translating all four vertices by the same vector translates the result by that vector; this is an affine average. The two edge endpoints receive more influence than the opposite corners. For a flat square split along a diagonal, the diagonal’s four surrounding vertices are symmetric around its midpoint, so this rule places the new point at that midpoint. On a curved neighborhood, it shifts the point according to both incident faces, which helps produce a smooth limit instead of merely inserting geometric midpoints.

Catmull–Clark: face, edge, and vertex masks

Catmull–Clark subdivision starts from a polygon mesh and turns every old face into quads. For each old face, insert a face point at the average of its vertices. For each old edge, insert an edge point. For an interior edge with endpoints and and adjacent face points and , use

This differs from an unweighted midpoint because the two face averages participate; the resulting weights remain symmetric across the edge. An edge on a boundary has only one adjacent face, so the interior formula is not defined there. In the common boundary-preserving variant, the new boundary point is the midpoint .

The old vertex update combines three kinds of local average. Let be the old vertex of valence (the number of incident edges), let be the average of the face points of its incident faces, and let be the average of the midpoints of its incident edges. The new position is

The coefficient gives the edge-midpoint average twice the weight of the face-point average; the old position’s coefficient grows with valence. For a regular interior quad vertex, , so . This is not the same as a plain average of the vertex and its neighbors: it incorporates the face averages and the topology around the vertex. Repeating the step creates a smoother surface. Starting from a quad mesh makes the regular valence four natural. Starting from a triangle mesh makes the typical valence six extraordinary for Catmull–Clark, which can produce irregular normal behavior; Loop is tailored to triangles. The course illustrates the difference with reflected lines and caustics: smooth normal variation produces smooth highlights, while many irregular vertices make the highlights appear jagged. This rule treats the boundary as a smooth curve and avoids applying the interior face-neighborhood mask where a face is missing. Extraordinary vertices—vertices whose valence differs from the regular valence of the scheme—need not disappear; the masks define their local limit behavior, but continuity and curvature can differ from regular patches. A subdivision implementation must handle these neighborhoods intentionally rather than assuming every vertex has the same number of faces.
Quadric error metric: turn nearby planes into a collapse cost

Mesh simplification reduces face count by repeatedly collapsing an edge. A greedy scheme assigns each candidate edge a cost, collapses the cheapest, updates local data, and repeats until it reaches a target size. The cost should estimate how much geometric detail is lost. The quadric error metric (QEM) approximates the distance from the replacement vertex to the planes of nearby triangles. It is a local approximation: it does not measure every possible global change, so implementations also need topology and orientation checks. The Fall 2020 slides derive it from point-to-plane distance and homogeneous coordinates. CMU-11 (PDF pp. 28–37; video 00:39:36–00:48:00)

A plane is described by a unit normal and a point on the plane. For query point , the signed distance is . Because has unit length, its absolute value is Euclidean distance. Expanding gives , where . Define homogeneous vectors and . The plane residual is . Squaring it gives
The fixed matrix is the plane’s quadric. “Quadric” means a quadratic function of the coordinates; here it is the squared plane residual. For a set of nearby face planes with matrices , add them once:

Each term penalizes distance from one plane. Summing matrices is valid because every plane contributes a quadratic form in the same homogeneous coordinate vector. The sum can therefore be stored as one matrix and evaluated cheaply for many possible replacement positions.

For each triangle, form its plane matrix. At each vertex, sum matrices for incident triangles to get vertex quadric . To consider collapsing an edge with endpoint vertices and , add their quadrics: . The new point should minimize this sum. Write the candidate position as and partition the homogeneous matrix so its cost has the form
where is a symmetric matrix, is a three-component vector, and is a scalar, all read from . The gradient with respect to is . At a stationary point it is zero, so solving

gives the unconstrained minimizing location when is positive definite. Positive definite means for every nonzero vector ; the quadratic then curves upward in every direction and has one unique minimum. Because is a sum of plane outer products , its block is , so is positive semidefinite in exact arithmetic; an indefinite indicates a sign, assembly, or numerical error in this unmodified QEM. If is singular, the minimizer may be nonunique, but the system remains consistent: lies in the range of , and the cost is constant along null directions. Near-singularity can still make a direct solve unstable in floating-point arithmetic. A rank-revealing SVD or pseudoinverse can find a minimum-norm solution; a robust simple fallback evaluates the cost at endpoint , endpoint , and their midpoint, then chooses the least-cost candidate. More elaborate implementations can add constraints or solve a constrained minimization problem.

For a numeric cost trace, take three unit-normal planes through the origin: , , and . Their point-to-plane squared distances sum to , so is the identity matrix, , and . A proposed edge-collapse point has cost . Solving gives the origin, whose cost is zero. In a real mesh, the planes are those of incident triangles, so their intersection may be approximate or empty; the computed point then finds a least-squares compromise rather than an exact shared intersection. Cost priorities can favor a point that is geometrically close to many local planes, but a low cost alone does not guarantee a valid triangle mesh.

The algorithm stores the chosen quadric at the merged vertex as the sum , updates costs for edges touching the changed neighborhood, and selects the next least-cost collapse. A candidate can invert a triangle even if its plane error is small. For each triangle incident to the proposed collapsed vertex, compare its old and proposed oriented normals; if their dot product is negative, the orientation has reversed, so reject that collapse. This protects local face orientation while the QEM handles geometric deviation. The two checks answer different questions: QEM scores shape change, while the normal test rejects a topological/geometric fold. CMU-11

Additional geometry notes for surfaces and parameterization
Subdivision meshes and the topology they need

A regular grid can be refined by corner cutting in two directions. Apply the one-quarter/three-quarter rule along u-edges, then v-edges, connect the new points into a denser quad mesh, and repeat. The number of cells grows quickly, but each refinement uses local averages and the mesh approaches a smooth limit. The source motivates the limit as a patch made from quadratic behavior in both parameter directions. A four-corner cell has the bilinear interpolant

At the result is ; at it is , and similarly for the other corners. The weights sum to one, so the patch is an affine combination. At all four weights are , giving the cell center. This formula is bilinear interpolation over one face; it helps calculate the child grid but should not be mistaken for the complete quadratic subdivision limit. (P3-16)

Regular quad grids are easy to store as an array: neighboring cells follow from index arithmetic. Real meshes are not always regular quads. A Doo–Sabin-style refinement begins with each face, creates updated points around it, and connects them into a smaller face; adjacent original faces contribute a quad across each shared edge, while the neighborhood around an original vertex becomes a polygon whose side count reflects that vertex’s valence. Repeating the process makes those exceptional polygons shrink, leaving regular quad regions between them. The lecture sketches the construction through face centers and radial midpoints and calls the exceptional neighborhoods extraordinary points. Canonical Doo–Sabin implementations use a specific face-valence-dependent averaging mask; the transcript’s geometric sketch is an intuition for topology and convergence, not a full rule table. (P3-16)

Catmull–Clark, introduced in the next lecture, produces cubic bicubic behavior in regular regions and is widely used in subdivision modeling. Doo–Sabin is associated with biquadratic pieces. In either family, one must keep the surface shape and the connectivity graph together: newly created vertices, face points and edge points change which faces meet at each edge. This is why subdivision is both geometry and a data-structure problem. (P3-16)

A split-edge (half-edge-style) record stores local mesh adjacency. One record represents one oriented side of an edge and points to its vertex, the next oriented edge around its face, and its opposite record across the same geometric edge. The face record points to one boundary edge; the vertex record can point to one incident edge. From these links, an iterator walks a face boundary or a vertex’s one-ring without duplicating vertex coordinates in every polygon. A shared vertex is stored once in a vertex array, while faces reference it through adjacency pointers. When subdivision replaces edges and faces, every reciprocal link must be updated. A stale opposite pointer or broken cycle can cause an invalid walk or crash. The old lecture calls this “pointer hell”; the durable lesson is to state topology invariants and test every adjacency update. Modern libraries may use indexed arrays instead, but they still represent the same relationships. (P3-16)
Catmull–Clark and Loop subdivision
Catmull–Clark turns a polygon mesh into a smoother, denser mesh by creating three kinds of local points on every pass:

ListItem.Content: A face point is the average of the face’s corner vertices. For a quad, .

An interior edge point is the average of the two edge endpoints and the face points on both sides: . For a boundary edge, there is only one adjacent face, so production schemes use a boundary rule (often the midpoint or a boundary-curve mask).

An updated old vertex point uses its surrounding face and edge neighborhood. For a regular interior vertex of valence , a common Catmull–Clark rule is , where averages adjacent face points and averages edge midpoints. For a regular quad grid (), this equals the familiar weighted average of the vertex, its four edge neighbors and four diagonal neighbors.

Chapter.Content: Once these points exist, connect them consistently: each old face becomes a face around its face point, each old edge creates a quad joining its edge point to nearby face and vertex points, and each old vertex gets a new incident face. A programmer can process faces, edges and vertices in separate passes because the formulas depend on those preceding values. This creates many new faces in one iteration; repeating the same local recipe approaches a smooth limit surface. (P3-16, P3-17)

The valence is the number of edges incident to a vertex. A regular quad-mesh vertex has valence four; a hand, nose or other irregular modeling feature may have a different valence. These extraordinary vertices have a different local limit behavior and are why the update weights cannot be chosen casually. The lecture reports a valence-dependent constant near , but it does not fully derive the standard mask. Use the explicit rule above only for the stated regular interior scheme, and consult the chosen subdivision standard for boundaries and extraordinary points. (P3-17)

For triangle meshes, Loop subdivision splits each triangle into four using edge points and then smooths the old vertices. Starting from an icosahedron gives a useful sphere approximation: 20 triangular faces become 80, then 320, then 1,280. Each new midpoint lies on the chord between old points, inside the sphere; normalize its vector from the center and scale to the radius to project it back onto the sphere. This is a distinct operation from Loop’s smoothing rule: projection gives a faceted sphere with vertices on the sphere, while Loop moves vertices according to a valence-dependent mask to form a smooth limit. The lecturer gives a old vertex plus average of neighboring edge points rule, which is the regular valence-six case, not the universal formula for every triangle vertex. (P3-17)
As-rigid-as-possible local shape preservation
Connect to: meshes and connectivity; Laplacian operators; shape deformation; numerical optimization.

As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) surface modeling asks a simple question: when a user moves a few handle vertices, can each small mesh neighborhood move as close to a rigid transform as possible? A rigid transform rotates and translates a patch but does not scale or shear it. A whole surface usually cannot remain exactly rigid while bending around new constraints. ARAP instead finds the deformation whose local patches deviate from rigidity as little as possible.

For each vertex , define a cell from its incident triangles and one-ring neighbors. For an edge from to neighbor , let the original edge be and its deformed version be . If this neighborhood moved rigidly, some rotation would satisfy for every neighbor. When it does not, measure the mismatch with

The total energy sums this residual over all cells. The weights matter: uniform weights can make the result depend on how triangles happen to be tessellated. The paper uses cotangent weights, , for angles opposite edge . These weights reduce mesh bias and connect the method to the cotangent Laplace–Beltrami operator.

The local rotations are unknown, as are the deformed vertex positions. ARAP alternates between two easier subproblems. First, hold the current positions fixed and find the best rotation for each cell. Form a weighted covariance matrix , compute its singular value decomposition , then set . If the determinant is negative, flip the singular-vector sign associated with the smallest singular value so the result is a proper rotation, not a reflection. This is the weighted orthogonal Procrustes problem: the rotation that best aligns the original edges with the deformed edges.
Second, hold the rotations fixed and solve for all vertex positions. Setting the energy gradient to zero gives, for each vertex,

The left side is the sparse cotangent Laplacian applied to the unknown deformed positions. Handle vertices are fixed to user-specified targets; static anchors remove global translation and rotation ambiguity. The Laplacian matrix depends only on the original mesh and constraints. The method factors it once, then reuses that factorization for each coordinate and each alternating step. It updates the right-hand side as the local rotations change. Because each substep minimizes the same energy over one variable group, the energy does not increase across alternating updates.

A practical example is bending a detailed bar by translating its handle. The user does not specify a handle rotation. Rotation-propagation methods that rely on an input rotation may not know how to twist nearby details. ARAP estimates the neighborhood rotations from the current geometry and finds a smooth field of rotations that best preserves edge lengths. A bar can bend while retaining its grooves and local shape. The result is not a physically simulated material: it is an editing energy that encodes a geometric preference.

Evidence and limits. The 2007 paper reports C++ experiments on a Pentium 4 2.16 GHz laptop. Its unoptimized implementation ran interactively at about 10–30 frames per second for regions of interest up to 10,000 vertices, typically using two or three iterations per edit. Reported relative root-mean-square edge-length errors were small in the tested edits, though a twist that constrained the bar’s height required some stretching. The nonlinear objective can have local minima, so a reasonable initialization matters; the prior interactive frame is the natural warm start. As the mesh is refined, the anchored Laplacian’s condition number and solve cost increase, which can require more iterations. Multiresolution acceleration is a proposed remedy, not a result of this implementation. The paper says the same local-edge energy extends to volumetric cells such as tetrahedra, but its experiments focus on surface editing.
Source: Sorkine and Alexa, “As-Rigid-As-Possible Surface Modeling” (2007), complete paper, PDF pp. 1–8. Primary PDF.
Field-aligned remeshing without a global parameterization
Connect to: mesh connectivity and geometry processing; surface curvature; local coordinate fields; multiresolution optimization.

Instant Field-Aligned Meshes creates triangle- or quad-dominant remeshes by solving for two local fields on a surface graph. The first field chooses edge directions. The second places the mesh vertices along those directions. Many global remeshing methods build a globally consistent parameterization before extracting a mesh. This paper instead works with discontinuous local fields and resolves their jumps as it goes. That avoids a global cut-and-parameterize stage and lets the same local operator work on triangle meshes or point clouds.

The input is a graph . A vertex stores a 3D position and a surface normal; edges encode mesh adjacency or, for point clouds, -nearest neighbors. Each edge receives a weight. The algorithm repeatedly updates a field value at one vertex from its neighbors, in a Gauss–Seidel-like local smoothing step. Unlike ordinary Laplacian smoothing, the values have symmetries: an unoriented cross has four equivalent directions, and a six-direction field has six. The algorithm must compare directions after trying the allowed discrete rotations.

For an -fold rotationally symmetric orientation field, each vertex stores one tangent representative . Its equivalent directions are rotations of by multiples of . A four-fold field, or 4-RoSy field, is a cross field suited to quad meshing. When comparing two neighbors, the algorithm selects the pair of equivalent rotations with the smallest angular difference, averages the aligned representatives with edge weights, projects back into the tangent plane, and normalizes. The paper uses an extrinsic comparison: it measures angle in 3D space instead of first rotating both directions into one vertex’s tangent plane. This makes the field respond to the embedded shape. On a cube, for example, it can align to corners and curved features without the user specifying curvature constraints. The paper contrasts this with intrinsic smoothness, which is simpler but may miss surface features unless extra alignment constraints are added.

After edge directions are chosen, a local position field places the lattice. Each vertex stores a representative local parameter position. Neighboring representatives can differ by integer lattice translations; the local comparison searches for the closest compatible representatives in their symmetry-related lattices. Those integer jumps are not an implementation nuisance: they record where the field is discontinuous and how many mesh edges separate neighboring representatives. A scale parameter sets the target edge length. The search is restricted to nearby candidate lattice points rather than solving an unbounded shortest-vector problem. Each local update averages aligned neighbor positions and rounds to the closest lattice representative near the input vertex.

A field can be locally smooth but the repeated Gauss–Seidel updates often get trapped in poor minima. The authors build a multiresolution hierarchy by merging adjacent vertices with similar normals and comparable dual areas. They optimize both fields from the coarsest graph to the original one, using six iterations per level in their reported results. The coarse graph has fewer degrees of freedom and can move across larger regions; its result is then interpolated to the next level as a starting point. The authors explicitly treat this as a practical hypothesis about neighboring levels, not a formal convergence guarantee.

The integer jumps around graph cycles reveal singularities. If their composition around a cycle is nonzero, the local field cannot return to its starting representative. In the orientation field, the singularity becomes a non-regular vertex in the output mesh. In the position field, a residual lattice shift inserts or removes an isoline. It can create triangles, pentagons, or T-junctions in a quad-dominant mesh. The method accepts additional singularities when they help improve element isotropy or reduce distortion; it does not try to eliminate all irregular vertices.

The output mesh is extracted from the graph of representative positions and integer jumps. Vertices that appear to represent the same output position are merged, prioritizing short candidate links and skipping conflicts. The output position and normal are weighted combinations of the contributing input samples, with closer samples receiving more weight. A greedy walk extracts faces from the remaining oriented edges. This is intentionally simple, but it can produce non-manifold output for very coarse meshes of detailed or high-genus surfaces. The authors remove offending edges or vertices when manifold output is required, which can leave artifacts. Because the method does not build a volumetric scalar field, holes in regions absent from a point cloud remain holes.

Brush tools constrain edge direction or make a position-field isoline follow a drawn stroke. A singularity attractor edits the integer jumps to move or collapse singularities. This editing operation is currently limited to triangle meshes and should be applied last: it freezes the discrete jumps and then optimizes only the continuous field values.

Published results and tradeoffs. The paper reports remeshing a 13-million-vertex scanned dragon into roughly 80,000-vertex outputs in about 67–71 seconds. It remeshes a 4.9-million-point cloud in 34.4 seconds using ten nearest neighbors. Its local method scales near-linearly in the presented tests and is much faster than the compared global methods. It often obtains more uniform elements and better feature alignment than its chosen baselines, but it introduces more singularities. Those are measured comparisons on the paper’s inputs and hardware. They do not establish equal quality for every topology or a guarantee of a manifold mesh.
Source: Jakob et al., “Instant Field-Aligned Meshes” (2015), complete paper body and conclusion, PDF pp. 1–15. Primary PDF.
From a scanned triangle soup to a mesh we can trust

A small 3D scan of a clay cup arrives as a list of triangles. Each triangle has three coordinates, perhaps a normal and a color, but the file does not say which triangle touches which, whether two nearby vertices are meant to be one vertex, or whether the dark circular opening is an intentional rim or a hole in the scan. On screen the soup can look like a cup. A renderer can draw it. Yet a renderer needs only three points per triangle; a geometry algorithm needs to know that one face follows another, which edges are shared, where the boundary runs, and whether the surface has a consistent inside and outside.

This difference between visible shape and encoded structure is the starting point for mesh topology. A polygon mesh carries at least two kinds of information. Geometry gives locations such as . Connectivity says which vertices form each edge and face, and how those pieces meet. Moving a vertex changes geometry without necessarily changing connectivity. Joining two coincident but separately indexed vertices changes connectivity even when the rendered coordinates remain almost identical. Many apparently mysterious failures are one of these two edits masquerading as the other.

A triangle soup repeats its three positions for every face. If two triangles are meant to meet, they may still hold separate copies of the same coordinate. This is convenient for interchange and rendering, but it does not offer an explicit edge-to-face or vertex-to-neighbor relation. An indexed face set shares vertex records and stores faces as indices; a halfedge structure adds directed adjacency so an algorithm can walk around a face or a vertex. The halfedge representation gives each undirected interior edge two oppositely directed halfedges. Their next and opposite relations support local traversal, while a boundary halfedge has no adjacent face or belongs to an explicit boundary loop, depending on the implementation.
A mesh is a neighborhood rule as well as a drawing

An abstract triangle is a set of three vertex identities; a geometric triangle is the flat region spanned by three non-collinear positions. A finite simplicial complex contains vertices, edges and triangles, includes every face of each simplex, and requires two simplices to intersect only along a shared face or not at all. For example, if a triangle is present, all three of its edges and all three of its vertices must also be present. Two triangles cannot cross in their interiors and still be a simplicial complex. This is a combinatorial definition; a geometric realization places those elements in space without violating the required intersections.

A surface is locally two-dimensional. Around an interior point there should be a neighborhood that looks like a disk; around a boundary point it should look like a half-disk. In a triangle mesh, a simple edge-incidence test is necessary: an interior edge has exactly two incident triangles, and a boundary edge has exactly one. An edge with three incident triangles is nonmanifold. But edge counts alone are not sufficient. At an interior manifold vertex, the incident triangles must form one circular fan; at a boundary manifold vertex, they must form one fan with two boundary ends. The link of a vertex—roughly, the small ring of directions and faces around it—should be a single cycle or a single interval, respectively.

Picture a bow-tie made of two disks that meet at one shared vertex. Every edge may have only one or two incident triangles, but the shared vertex has two disjoint fans. It is not a manifold point: a tiny neighborhood is two disks touching at a point, not one disk or half-disk. A “butterfly” vertex link test catches this case. Likewise, two sheets that meet along an edge make an edge with more than two incident faces. A connected component is instead a whole island of faces reachable from one another through shared edges (or under a deliberately chosen vertex-adjacency rule). A boundary is not the same as a crack: a legitimate open surface has boundary edges; a crack may be two disconnected edge sets whose positions nearly coincide but whose vertex identities differ.

The distinction between geometry and topology also applies to self-intersection. A connected, manifold mesh can fold through itself in 3D while its abstract adjacency remains manifold. Conversely, a mesh with no visible self-crossing may have a nonmanifold edge or bow-tie vertex. A topology test cannot certify geometric embedding, and an intersection test cannot certify manifold neighborhoods. A robust pipeline reports these separately.

Orientation is a consistent choice of direction for each face. For an oriented triangle , its oriented boundary traverses , , and , with signs fixed by the chosen convention. If two neighboring faces are consistently oriented, they traverse their shared edge in opposite directions. Propagating this condition over a connected component either assigns consistent face orientations or discovers a contradiction, as on a nonorientable surface. In a closed orientable triangle mesh, consistent orientation supports a coherent normal direction. A mesh with a boundary can still be orientable; the boundary simply remains exposed.

Normals depend on geometry and orientation. Swapping two triangle vertices reverses its normal while leaving the triangle’s location unchanged. A bag of faces with arbitrary winding can shade inconsistently and makes inside/outside tests unreliable. Orientation propagation can fix a consistent winding when the mesh is orientable, but it cannot decide which side the application wants to call “outside” without an additional convention, such as signed volume for a closed embedded shell or a known camera/seed point. Nonorientable surfaces such as the Möbius strip cannot have a globally consistent face-normal direction, even though each local patch is perfectly regular.

Topology has different failure modes from geometric quality. A zero-area triangle, a needle with a very short edge, an inverted element, or a self-intersection may be geometrically dangerous while the incidence structure remains manifold. A single edge with three incident faces is topologically nonmanifold even if its triangles are all well-shaped. Keep separate diagnostics for incidence, vertex links, orientation, degeneracy, and self-intersection; repairing one does not imply the others are repaired.
The boundary of a boundary cancels

A useful way to turn connectivity into algebra is to treat a collection of vertices, edges, or triangles as a formal sum called a chain. For a triangle , using integer coefficients and an orientation, define
The signs encode direction: is the same directed edge as . The boundary operator extends by addition to a collection of faces. Now apply the edge-boundary operator to each term:

Every corner cancels. Informally, the edge boundary of a filled triangle has no leftover endpoint. The same principle applies to a triangulated patch: internal edges are traversed once in each direction by adjacent oriented faces and cancel; only the outside rim remains. This is the chain-level statement , “the boundary of a boundary is empty.” It is not a slogan pasted onto a mesh; it follows directly from the fact that each codimension-two face of a simplex occurs twice with opposite sign.

With coefficients modulo two, signs disappear because . Each edge of a triangle appears twice after taking the boundary twice, so it cancels in pairs. Modulo-two chains are often easier for a first computation: a chain can be represented as a set of simplices, and addition is symmetric difference. But mod two forgets orientation signs and cannot distinguish some orientation-sensitive phenomena. For integer coefficients, the plus and minus directions carry more information.
For a concrete disk, split a square with corners along diagonal . Its two faces are and . Their sum has boundary

because the shared diagonal appears as in one face and in the other. Thus the two-triangle patch has exactly the four-edge square boundary. If the same faces are wrapped and glued so every edge is shared consistently, every edge cancels and the surface is closed. This gives a practical orientation check: accumulate directed edge uses; interior edges should cancel, while boundary edges should occur once with a coherent loop direction.

A chain is a cycle when its boundary is zero. A boundary is a chain that is itself the boundary of a higher-dimensional chain. Every boundary is a cycle because . A loop that bounds a filled disk in the mesh is a 1-cycle that is also a 1-boundary. A loop around a tunnel may be a cycle but not the boundary of any mesh triangles. Homology records cycles up to the addition of boundaries, which is a compact way of distinguishing loops that can be filled from loops that cannot.
Euler characteristic is a structural checksum, not a shape score
For a finite triangle mesh, count vertices , edges , and faces . Its Euler characteristic is

The alternating signs matter. Splitting one triangle by adding a vertex in its interior produces three triangles and three new edges: , so . Splitting an edge shared by two triangles adds one vertex, three edges and two faces, again preserving . These local calculations explain why subdivision changes resolution without changing Euler characteristic. For a valid finite triangulation of the same surface, is independent of how finely it is triangulated.

A two-triangle square disk has four vertices, five edges and two faces, so . A tetrahedron surface is a sphere triangulation with four vertices, six edges and four faces, giving . There are vertices; horizontal and vertical edges contribute , the diagonals contribute , so ; each square contributes two triangles, so . Therefore . The counts assume periodic identifications form a valid simplicial torus without duplicated/degenerate simplex identities; the lower bound on grid size avoids the pathologies of collapsing too many periodic vertices together.

Here genus counts handles: a cup with one through-tunnel has genus one after it is closed; an open disk removed from a sphere contributes one boundary loop and lowers by one. For a connected nonorientable compact surface with cross-cap count and boundary loops, the corresponding formula is . A mesh does not reveal which formula applies until connectedness, compactness, manifoldness, orientability, and boundary loops have been checked.

For multiple components, Euler characteristic adds across components. But an unexplained count alone is ambiguous: could describe one sphere or two disks; invalid connectivity may also produce a coincidental expected count. The formula is useful as a checksum after structural classification, not as a certificate that a mesh is a sphere. It says nothing about triangle shape, embedded self-intersections, physical dimensions, or whether a small handle is a scan artifact.
The same count can be written using Betti numbers, the number of independent homology classes in each dimension:

For a finite 2D complex, counts connected components, counts independent nonfillable loops, and counts independent closed 2D shells. A disk has , hence . A sphere has and . A torus has and : it has two independent loop directions, around the tube and through the hole. These descriptions assume ordinary homology over a field or the corresponding ranks; torsion information in general integer homology is not represented by Betti numbers alone.
Homology: ask which loops actually have a filling

The algebra can be understood with a practical question. Imagine a wire loop drawn on a triangulated surface. Is it the edge boundary of some set of triangles? If yes, it can be filled within the represented surface. If not, it winds around a genuine topological feature—or the mesh is missing data or has an invalid neighborhood. Homology groups formalize this question dimension by dimension, but an engineer can first use the idea without needing to memorize group theory.

At dimension zero, vertices are connected by edges. The number of independent groups of vertices after all edges are considered is , the component count. At dimension one, edge cycles are loops. Loops that bound triangle patches count as trivial; the remaining independent classes contribute to . At dimension two, a closed collection of oriented triangles with no exposed edge boundary can form a 2-cycle. On a closed orientable surface the whole surface is one such class, contributing ; on a disk, the outer rim is exposed so there is no 2-cycle of the whole patch and .

This interpretation also clarifies a common language trap. “Hole” can mean a missing patch in a disk, a tunnel through a solid, a boundary loop, or a cavity in an embedded volume. These are different objects and appear in different dimensions of homology. The cup’s opening is a boundary component of its surface; a tunnel through a closed shell creates a nonfillable loop on the surface. Before reporting “number of holes,” state the represented space and the homology dimension.

A triangle boundary example is a small homology computation. Take the square disk with diagonal . The outside loop is the boundary of the two-face chain , so that loop represents zero in . On the torus, the loop along one periodic grid direction is not the boundary of a patch of torus triangles by itself; neither is a loop in the independent crossing direction. They generate two independent 1D classes. A contractible little loop around a single vertex is a cycle but is filled by the star patch around that vertex, so it is not an additional handle.

The count relationship is useful because it connects a cheap combinatorial statistic to the “cycles that remain after fillings” view. A discrepancy between the count and a separately computed Betti-number alternating sum can indicate an implementation error in boundary matrices, an inconsistent simplex ordering, or a mistake in component or boundary treatment. Agreement is still not proof of correct geometry: two wrong calculations can agree, and Euler characteristic is a coarse invariant.
Alpha complexes turn a union of balls into a finite topological object
A point cloud has no edges, faces, or loops until a scale rule is introduced. One geometric choice places a closed ball of radius around every sample. The union
is a continuous shape whose topology changes as grows. Directly storing and analyzing the union is awkward, so computational topology seeks a finite complex with the same relevant topology.
Intersect each ball with its Voronoi cell,
Each is convex. The alpha complex is the nerve of this convex cover:

Because every restricted cell lies inside its Voronoi cell, the alpha complex is a subcomplex of the Delaunay complex. The nerve theorem supplies the key bridge: under the convex-cover conditions, the combinatorial nerve has the same homotopy type as the union it represents.

This is more than a convenient point-cloud triangulation. The radius becomes an explicit geometric scale. At tiny radius the complex contains isolated vertices. Edges enter as restricted balls meet, then triangles and tetrahedra fill cycles and cavities. The nested family
is therefore a natural filtration for persistent homology.

Delaunay sparsity also matters computationally. A Čech complex built from all intersecting ball subsets can become combinatorially large. Alpha complexes retain only simplices compatible with Voronoi/Delaunay geometry, often giving a much smaller complex while still representing the union-of-balls topology.

For scanned geometry, the interpretation must remain honest. Radius is not “noise level” by definition. Nonuniform sampling, anisotropic sensor uncertainty, missing regions, and outliers can make one global radius physically inappropriate. The complex faithfully answers the topology of the chosen union-of-balls model, not the unknown true surface without assumptions.
Source basis: Edelsbrunner and Harer, Computational Topology: An Introduction, Chapter III, especially the Delaunay and alpha-complex construction and the union-of-balls/nerve interpretation.
Persistence asks which features survive scale changes

A scan has noise at several scales. Some short loops arise from tiny ripples; other holes belong to the cup’s structure. A single topology count cannot say whether a loop is a persistent feature or a small perturbation. A filtration makes scale explicit: build a nested sequence of complexes by increasing a parameter, and track when each component, loop, or shell appears and when it becomes filled or merged.

One useful construction begins with sample points and a distance scale . At a small scale each sample is isolated. As grows, nearby samples connect; groups merge into components, loops appear when edges close cycles, and loops disappear when filled faces enter. An alpha complex is a computationally efficient subcomplex related to unions of balls around sample points. Another option is a sublevel filtration of a scalar field on an already triangulated surface: assign a value to each vertex and add a simplex when its highest-valued vertex is reached, ensuring all faces of a simplex have already appeared. The choice of function and filtration determines what “scale” means.

A feature has a birth parameter and a death parameter. Their difference, persistence, is its lifetime in the filtration. In a diagram, each feature is a point above the diagonal, and its vertical distance is persistence. A tiny noisy loop that appears and fills over a narrow range is often short-lived. The cup’s larger opening-related feature may survive across a much wider range. The diagram is a diagnostic of scale-stability, not a truth oracle: an intentionally small handle can also be short-lived, and a long-lived artifact caused by a systematic scan gap can look significant.

For a tiny explicit example, add three vertices of a triangle first, then its three edges, then its face. The first two edges join the vertices into one component; the third edge closes a loop and creates a 1-cycle; the triangle then fills that cycle. Each isolated vertex births a connected component. As edges merge components, an elder-rule pairing kills the younger component classes; one oldest component remains as an essential ordinary class when the completed triangle is connected. With tied birth values, a fixed tie-breaking order chooses the representative without changing the persistence multiset. The 1D feature is born at the edge that closes the loop and dies when the face arrives. If filtration values are for vertices, edges, and face, respectively, the 1D lifetime is only about in the selected scale. That number is meaningful only relative to units, sampling density and the filtration rule.

In a simplicial filtration, simplex values must be monotone with inclusion: a face cannot arrive after its coface. Persistence algorithms encode the boundary of each simplex as a column in a boundary matrix, then reduce columns in order so repeated lowest rows are eliminated. A zero reduced column corresponds to a cycle-birth event; a nonzero column pairs with the simplex that kills a class. The matrix view explains why adding the triangle kills the loop it bounds. It also makes clear why a boundary operator must satisfy : without that, the algebraic events would not describe cycles and fillings consistently.

Persistence is often presented as robust to small perturbations, but translating that theorem into a mesh cleanup threshold requires care. The theorem concerns a specified function and metric, with a chosen distance between diagrams; it does not say that every short-lived feature is noise or that every significant geometric defect will be detected. An engineering workflow should show the filtration parameter, its physical or normalized units, the sampling assumptions, coefficient field, persistence threshold and a visual or analytic justification. Preserve the persistence diagram or feature list as diagnostic evidence rather than silently deleting geometry.
Persistence stability says small function perturbations cannot move the diagram arbitrarily far

A persistence diagram is useful as a measurement only if a small perturbation of the measured function does not cause arbitrary topological chaos in the output. Edelsbrunner and Harer make this precise with the bottleneck metric.
For two persistence diagrams and , augment each with diagonal points so short-lived features can be matched to the diagonal. The bottleneck distance is
where ranges over bijections respecting multiplicity. It asks for the matching whose worst paired displacement is as small as possible.
For monotone filtration functions and on the same complex, the stability theorem gives

A corresponding theorem is developed for tame continuous functions on triangulable spaces. The important claim is quantitative: if every function value moves by at most , then no persistence point needs to move by more than in bottleneck distance.

This does not say every short-persistence feature is noise. It says the representation is stable with respect to perturbations measured in a specified norm of a specified function. A genuine tiny handle can have low persistence. A large systematic scan gap can have high persistence. Choosing a deletion threshold is still a domain decision.

The theorem is nevertheless valuable in a repair pipeline. If two depth reconstructions differ by a known bounded scalar-field perturbation, their persistence diagrams cannot disagree arbitrarily under the theorem’s conditions. Conversely, a diagram change much larger than the known perturbation scale suggests that some assumption changed—domain, filtration, registration, topology construction, or error bound—not merely tiny numerical noise.

A practical validation should therefore store the filtration function and its units alongside the diagram. Comparing diagrams without recording whether was height, distance-to-samples, curvature, confidence, or density makes the stability number uninterpretable.
Source basis: Computational Topology, Chapter VIII on bottleneck/Wasserstein distances and the stability theorems for filtrations and tame functions.
Morse functions and Reeb graphs compress how level-set components split and merge
Persistent homology summarizes births and deaths of algebraic features. A Reeb graph keeps a different piece of information: how connected components of a scalar function’s level sets evolve.
Given a continuous function

two points are considered equivalent when they lie in the same connected component of the same level set. Quotienting by that equivalence gives the Reeb graph . Each point of the graph represents one contour/level-set component.

This is useful for iso-surface extraction. Instead of scanning an entire volume to discover every component of , the Reeb graph can identify how many contour components exist at level and provide representatives from which each component can be traced. When the domain is contractible, as in a cube volume, the Reeb graph is a tree and is often called a contour tree.

For a Morse function on a manifold, critical points organize the graph. A local minimum creates a new level-set component; a saddle can merge or split components; a maximum destroys the final local component. On an orientable 2-manifold, minima/maxima correspond to degree-one nodes and the relevant saddles to degree-three nodes. Thus the topology of the scalar field becomes a one-dimensional combinatorial object.

The height function on a torus is the canonical mental model. Starting below the torus gives an empty sublevel set. Passing the lowest critical point creates a disk. A saddle changes it to a cylinder, another saddle changes the connectivity again, and the maximum completes the torus. The critical values mark where topology changes; between them, level-set structure is stable.

Reeb graphs are lossy summaries. They preserve component evolution and some one-dimensional connectivity, not the full topology or metric geometry. Edelsbrunner and Harer show, for example, that and . A graph is therefore useful for navigation through level sets and segmentation, but it should not replace a full homology/persistence computation when higher-dimensional features matter.

In graphics/vision, choose to match the question: height for terrain, scalar density for volumetric imaging, geodesic distance for shape segmentation, curvature-like fields for surface decomposition, or confidence/error fields for reconstruction diagnostics. The graph summarizes that function on that domain, not shape in an absolute sense.
Source basis: Computational Topology, Chapter VI on Morse functions, piecewise-linear critical points, Reeb graphs/contour trees, and the relationship between graph nodes and critical points.
The discrete Laplacian turns adjacency into a motion rule
Once neighborhoods are trustworthy, the mesh can approximate differential operators. A scalar function lives at vertex . A simple uniform graph Laplacian compares it with its one-ring neighbors:

This asks whether the center differs from its neighboring average. It depends only on connectivity, not on edge lengths or triangle areas. On an irregularly sampled planar mesh, a linear coordinate field can have a nonzero uniform Laplacian even though the smooth plane’s Laplacian is zero.
